extracted.intended_audience: literate readers of early-18th-century periodical essays interested in morals, manners, religion, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical moral essays and letters (The Spectator-style) offering evaluative maxims about modesty, religion (faith vs. morality), vanity, pleasantry, and social behaviour in early-18th-century England. The page mixes short essays and reader-letters advancing prescriptive judgments about conduct and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Modesty vs False Modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: "True Modesty is ashamed to do any thing that is repugnant to the Rules of right Reason: False Modesty is ashamed to do any thing that is opposite to the Humour of the Company."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True Modesty: an instinct limited by prudence and religion, guards virtue and avoids what is criminal. False Modesty: a vague instinct governed by fashion, leads one to conform to company even when actions are indiscreet or criminal. Examples/anti-patterns: lending money you cannot spare, signing as surety for acquaintances you dislike, giving recommendations for strangers, living contrary to your own judgment, complying with immoral company-ways. Anecdote: Xenophanes preferred appearing 'timorous' to risking immoral conduct; false-modesty persons 'fall in with the Torrent.' Moral: do not let shame of singularity override reason and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Modesty as a source of religious decline in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: False modesty (shame of being devout) has contributed to the wearing away of outward expressions of Christianity in ordinary life and conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical diagnosis: reaction against sectarian hypocrisy after the Rebellion made visible devotion suspect; ridicule of seriousness pushed society to the opposite extreme where any appearance of devotion is 'out of Countenance.' Practical implication: public shame about devotion is socially produced and harms the appearance of religion; remedy is to distinguish hypocrisy (detestable) from public concealment of true piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sincere virtue yet let the world see you are virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: "The due Mean to be observed is to be sincerely Virtuous, and at the same time to let the World see we are so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance: hypocrisy is worse for the individual, but open impiety is more pernicious socially; therefore practice virtue sincerely but also allow visible marks of virtue so society is not misled. Biblical/authoritative threat used as deterrent against perverted modesty (being ashamed before men about important matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion comprises two heads: Faith and Morality; a perfect person needs both
rubrics_metrics.description: "Religion may be considered under two General Heads... By those things which we are to believe... I shall distinguish by the Name of Faith, the Second by that of Morality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarification of terms: Faith = revealed doctrines not discoverable by natural light; Morality = duties dictated by reason or natural religion. A 'perfect Man' should not be defective in either. The essay enumerates reasons why Morality has pre-eminence (six points) — e.g., much of morality is of fixed eternal nature, gives greater perfection to human nature, is more certain across civilized nations, and a virtuous infidel may be saved where a vicious believer is not. It also lists ways Faith enhances Morality (explain/heighten moral points; furnish stronger motives; give more amiable ideas of the Supreme Being; demonstrate blackness of vice; serve as ordinary method of making morality effectual to salvation). Practical implication: cultivate both, but understand their different roles and mutual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims about belief and its relation to morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit maxims on the relation of belief to moral effect: (1) "That we should be particularly cautious of making any thing an Article of Faith, which does not contribute to the Confirmation or Improvement of Morality." (2) "That no Article of Faith can be true and authentick, which weakens or subverts the practical part of Religion." (3) "That the greatest Friend of Morality... cannot possibly apprehend any Danger from embracing Christianity, as it is preserved pure and uncorrupt in the Doctrines of our National Church."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: theological propositions should be evaluated by their moral consequences; do not accept articles of faith that would undermine practical virtue. Use consequential thinking in doubtful points: consider harm before assenting, especially when principles produce evident injury (example: prosecuting men for conscience's sake produces hatred, affliction, familial ruin). The essay urges near-mathematical certainty before acting on doubtful principles that would harm neighbors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider consequences before embracing disputed religious principles
rubrics_metrics.description: In doubtful points of faith or conscience, consider the ill consequences that may arise from them (if erroneous) before giving assent or acting upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: prosecuting men for conscience may embitter minds, cause hatred and resentment, enforce professions of false belief, cut people off from society, afflict bodies and fortunes, hurt reputations and families, and possibly end lives. Practical rule: require high certainty (comparable to mathematical demonstration) before adopting or executing principles with such harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity and the 'Paradise of Fools' — beware flattering public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity, popular opinion, and self-conceit create a delusive 'Palace of Vanity' where people mistake follies and extravagant actions for merit and glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symptoms/anti-patterns: seeking praise, imitating fashions, surrounding oneself with flatterers, affecting outward ornamentation, confusing seeming merit with real worth. Social mechanics: Opinion and Error work together (Opinion flatters, Error disguises as truth), Flattery/Affectation/Fashion sustain vanity. Consequences: humiliation by Scorn, Poverty, Trouble; the apparent glory is unsupported—foundation like 'curling Clouds' and may collapse. Remedy: plain-dealing and sensible self-esteem; beware the house of Vanity and its harpies; be cautious of self-praise and mutual praise among company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-dealing versus fashionable ridicule — consequences for truth-tellers
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain-dealing (speaking truth or correcting vanity) is often met with scorn, calumny (called 'Envy' or 'Slander'), and social exclusion by Vanity's followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social penalty: those who complain of the management of mankind by opinion and vanity are driven out, slighted by Vanity, and labelled by Flattery/Affectation/Fashion. Despite this, plain-dealing provides warning about the future fall of vain people; readers are urged to heed such warnings even if unpopular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church behaviour: avoid theatrical ceremonies and salutations during worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Letterer's critique: Ceremonies, bows, courtesies, whisperings, smiles, winks, nods, and other familiar arts of salutation in churches occupy time that should be devoted to the duty and true intent of religious assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative examples: Roman Catholic and Mahometan congregations observed to show greater propriety by not attentively acknowledging personal acquaintances during worship — suggested as patterns to imitate. Practical recommendation: enter religious assemblies solemnly engaged rather than treating them like theatres; avoid using the time to catalogue fashions or dress of attendees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry: valuable with virtue, dangerous as a cover for vice
rubrics_metrics.description: "People are not aware of the very great Force which Pleasantry in Company has... His Faults are generally overlooked..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pleasantry accompanies manly and virtuous sentiments it is highly pleasing; but when it stands alone it 'gilds a Crowd of ill Qualities' and such 'pleasant Fellows' should be avoided. Dangers include breaking promises, ill-nature in domestic relations, turning others into jokes, debauching women, and using wit to mask selfishness. Social effect: pleasant behaviour often excuses moral laxity; be wary of accepting social charm as moral evidence. Historical illustration: Charles II's gaiety was socially useful in moderation, but the pleasant temper can be abused by flatterers and corrupt use of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride renders us susceptible to flattery and disguise of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride is ubiquitous, appears in many disguises, and when misapplied makes people open to flatterers who gain access to their souls and influence their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride can be virtuous if rightly applied, but more often opens avenues for manipulation. Example: King Charles II's easy accessability gratified public vanity and could be exploited. Practical implication: watch pride's manifestations, and do not let desire for esteem lead to being misled by flatterers.
